extracted.intended_audience: aspiring literary critics, reviewers, and playwrights (educated readers interested in criticism and drama)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and producing poetry, tragedy, and literary criticism — covering what a critic should know and how a dramatist should construct characters, sentiments, and stage representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four heads for judging epic/poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a poem under the four great heads of the Fable, the Characters, the Sentiments, and the Language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four dimensions form a comprehensive framework for criticism; Milton is said to excel under each. Use them as distinct axes when assessing an epic or long poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's prerequisite — knowledge of ancient and modern authors
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic should be acquainted not only with French and Italian critics but also with the Ancient and Moderns who have written in the learned languages; above all, well versed in the Greek and Latin poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without this background a reader often fancies he understands criticism but miscomprehends it. Familiarity with classical models supplies methodized reflections and perfects private critical hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's prerequisite — clear logical head and the art of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic must have a clear and logical head to avoid being puzzled or perplexed amidst his own blunders, and to convey thoughts with clearness and perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle combined excellence in criticism with excellence in logic; lacking logical skill leads to confused thinking, mistaken senses of those one would confute, or inability to communicate right judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's prerequisite — breadth of learning (distinguish words and things)
rubrics_metrics.description: An author or critic should know how to distinguish between words and things and to range and set his thoughts in proper lights (Locke's teaching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignorance of common arts and sciences and of the difference between words and ideas leads to confusion and illiterate criticism; the art of ordering thoughts prevents obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic should praise excellencies and discover concealed beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: A true critic ought to dwell rather upon Excellencies than Imperfections, to discover the concealed Beauties of a Writer, and communicate things worth observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fixating on little faults; many ordinary readers immediately ridicule passages but a judicious critic digs below the surface (cf. 'Errors, like Straws... He who would search for Pearls must dive below').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attacking or ridiculing 'glowing bold expressions' (verbum ardens)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very easy to brand a 'verbum ardens' or glowing bold expression as ridiculous by cold ill-natured criticism; a critic should not make such passages the butt of ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such ridicule is unfair and may turn beauty into derision. Recognize that the most exquisite words and strokes are often most doubtful to those lacking a relish for polite learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on ridicule or misplaced wit in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirth and wit in a critic are unseasonable when used in improper places; showing wit where it is improper prejudices the reader and can unjustly expose beauties to derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wit sparingly and with judgment; being merry at the wrong time shows impertinence and may indicate a critic more in love with his talent for ridicule than with fair judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being an illiterate critic who praises only what the public already applauds
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark of a critic without taste nor learning is that he seldom ventures to praise any passage not already received and applauded by the public, and his criticism turns wholly upon little faults and errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such critics often base judgments on received opinion and petty faults; true criticism should find and promote unnoticed excellencies rather than merely echo public applause or point out trifling mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value genius over scrupulous exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Productions of a great genius, with many lapses and inadvertencies, are infinitely preferable to the works of an inferior kind of author which are scrupulously exact and conformable to all rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating works, prioritize overall greatness and creative force over mere technical perfection; do not let formal exactness outweigh imaginative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should represent truth and humane life in its incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy ought to represent truth and humane life in the incidents which concern heroes and heroines, so that passions dwell strongly on the imagination and move even professional dissemblers to real tears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for situations grounded in believable human motives and virtues; evoke authentic passion rather than mere theatrical affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandeur of character shown by greatness of sentiment, not stage trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: Grandeur in characters should appear in greatness of Sentiments flowing from minds worthy their condition, not by directing that guards and waiters follow them in every scene or by external ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on costume, stage furniture, or ostentatious stage business to indicate worth; instead, build characters whose thoughts and maxims of conduct demonstrate their rank and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters and misfortunes founded on virtue, not mere weakness or vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in tragedy should be laudable; their misfortunes should arise from unguarded Virtue rather than a propensity to Vice or from mere weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design protagonists so that their suffering elicits sympathy and moral instruction—virtue tested by calamity is more moving and imitable than distress that reveals moral deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic virtues and universal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic virtues (e.g., a mother's care, fidelity to a deceased husband) concern all the world and make characters imitable and affecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground tragic sentiment in universally recognizable domestic duties and affections to reach a broad audience's sympathies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt stage business and costuming to contemporary taste
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy current tastes, scenes should be busy enough and parts perfectly newly dressed; stage business and fresh costumes can gain favour with certain classes of critics and audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not substituting ornament for substance, be mindful that staging and costume contribute to audience reception; balance theatrical novelty with natural representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor authenticity — feeling and restraint in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors who read or perform may be strongly moved by the passions they represent (e.g., throwing down the book, shedding tears); genuine humanity in performance enhances the audience's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage performances that allow authentic feeling but remain within the bounds of decency and the rules of good-breeding so the audience perceives real passion without offensive excess.
